title: Basic Nursery Production Processes and Systems

lessons.title: The nursery as a production system
lessons.html:
Seeing the whole flow

A production nursery works like a factory with living products. Raw materials come in, go through a series of processes, and leave as saleable plants. If one step is late or poor, every step after it suffers. A supervisor must understand the whole system, not only one section.

Main processes in order

  1. Receiving inputs: seed, cuttings, plugs, growing media, containers, fertiliser and labels arrive and are checked against the order.
  2. Propagation: sowing, sticking cuttings or weaning tissue-culture plants.
  3. Transplanting or potting: young plants move into their final or intermediate container.
  4. Growing on: irrigation, feeding, spacing, pruning and pest control until the plant reaches size.
  5. Hardening off and finishing: preparing the plant for the customer, cleaning pots and labelling.
  6. Order picking, dispatch and sales: selecting, packing and loading plants onto trolleys, bakkies or trucks.

Support systems

Behind these processes sit support systems: water supply and irrigation, the potting shed, the chemical store, workshops, stock control, record keeping and staff management. A broken borehole pump or an empty fertiliser store can stop production as surely as a disease outbreak.

Inputs, outputs and losses

Every process has inputs (materials, labour, water, time) and outputs (plants moved to the next stage). The difference between what goes in and what comes out good is loss: seeds that did not germinate, cuttings that did not root, plants that died or were thrown away as unsaleable. Measuring loss at each stage tells the nursery where to improve. For example, if 1 000 cuttings are stuck and 850 root, the strike rate is 85%.

Thinking in systems helps you answer practical questions: How many cuttings must we stick today to deliver 5 000 shrubs in six months? Where is the bottleneck holding up the flow? Which stage loses the most plants?

lessons.title: Production scheduling and crop timing
lessons.html:
Working back from the sale date

Nursery plants take weeks or months to grow, so production must be planned well before the customer wants the plants. The usual method is to work backwards from the date of sale.

Example: spring bedding plants

A garden centre orders 2 000 trays of petunias for the first week of September. If the crop takes about ten weeks from sowing to sale in your conditions, sowing must happen in late June. If you normally lose 10% along the way, you must sow enough to finish with 2 000 good trays, not just 2 000.

StageTypical taskPlanned week
SowingFill plug trays, sow, labelWeek 1
TransplantMove plugs into traysWeek 4
Growing onFeed, pinch, spaceWeeks 5 to 9
DispatchPick, clean, loadWeek 10

The weeks in this table are an example only; real timing depends on the plant, season and your own records.

Why timing changes

Crops grow faster in warm weather and slower in winter. A tunnel or heated house speeds growth. Day length affects flowering in some plants, such as chrysanthemums and poinsettias. Good nurseries keep records of how long each crop took in each season, and use those records for the next plan.

Production schedules

Managers turn orders and stock targets into a production schedule that lists what to sow, stick, pot or space each week. The supervisor receives this schedule and turns it into daily tasks for the team. If something cannot be done on time, such as late seed delivery, report it immediately so the plan can be adjusted.

lessons.title: Records, stock control and quality systems
lessons.html:
Knowing what you have and how good it is

A nursery can have hundreds of thousands of plants. Without good records nobody knows what is available to sell, what is ready, or what went wrong.

Batch labelling and records

Every batch should carry a label or tag with the plant name, variety, date sown or stuck, quantity and batch number. The same information goes into the nursery record book or computer system. As the batch moves through stages, record transplant dates, quantities moved, losses, sprays and feeds applied.

Stock control

  • Count stock regularly, by block or bench.
  • Record plants moved, sold, or thrown away the same day.
  • Mark stock as not ready, ready or reserved for an order.
  • Keep input stock (media, pots, fertiliser) at levels that will not stop production.

Quality standards

Customers buy on appearance. Most nurseries set standards for each product: minimum height or spread, number of shoots, root development, leaf colour, no pests or disease, clean container and correct label. Plants are graded against these standards before dispatch. Plants that fall short are held back to grow on, sold as a lower grade, or discarded.

Hygiene and biosecurity systems

Incoming plants can bring pests and diseases. Keep new stock apart until checked, clean trolleys and trays between batches, and control who walks from dirty areas into the propagation house. Report any unusual pest or disease to the manager straight away.

Health and safety systems

The OHS Act 85 of 1993 requires the employer to provide a safe workplace and workers to follow safe procedures. In the nursery this includes safe chemical storage, protective equipment, safe lifting of heavy pots, and safe use of potting machines.

Key points

  • The nursery is a chain of processes: inputs, propagation, potting, growing on, finishing and dispatch.
  • Plan production backwards from the sale date and allow for losses.
  • Label and record every batch so that stock and losses are known.
  • Grade plants against clear quality standards before dispatch.
  • Hygiene and safety systems protect plants and people.

By working forward from the day seed arrives
